items.prompt: Explain why the four elements of the marketing mix are decided together rather than one at a time.
items.canonical_answer: Because each element signals something to the buyer and buyers read the signals together. A premium product priced high but promoted with discount flyers and sold from a market stall gives contradictory signals, and buyers tend to resolve the contradiction downwards, so the position the business wanted is lost. The elements also constrain one another in practice: choosing to sell through supermarkets rather than one shop makes packaging carry the explanation, lowers the price the producer receives because the retailer takes a margin, and changes what promotion has to do.
marking_guidance: The reason must be that the elements are read together by buyers and constrain one another.
Reward an example in which one element undermines another.
A list of the four elements without saying why they interact does not answer the question.

items.prompt: Namib Fresh sells tomatoes either pre-packed to a supermarket chain or loose at a Saturday market in Otjiwarongo. Explain how the change of outlet changes the other three elements of its marketing mix.
items.canonical_answer: Through the chain, the product becomes a graded 500 g punnet with a barcode because nobody is present to explain it; the price for each kilogram is lower because the chain negotiates and takes its own margin; and promotion is reduced to the pack and the shelf position. At the market the product is loose fruit picked the day before; the price for each kilogram is higher because no intermediary takes a share; and promotion is the stall, the grower's presence and word of mouth. The tomato is the same in both cases, so the facts that change the answer are the outlet and who stands between grower and buyer.
marking_guidance: The context supplied - the supermarket chain and the Saturday market - must do the work; a general account of the 4Ps does not answer it.
The reasoning must link the outlet to each of the other three elements, because the retailer's margin and the absence of a salesperson are what force the changes.
Must reach the conclusion that one decision about place has changed product, price and promotion.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a good and a service.
items.canonical_answer: A good is a physical item that can be made in advance, stored, owned and resold - a bag of maize meal. A service is an act performed for a customer, produced at the moment it is used - a haircut or a bus journey. Because of that, a service cannot be inspected before it is bought, capacity not used at the time cannot be kept for later, the person delivering it is part of what is bought, and it is harder to repeat identically.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required, with at least one consequence that follows from it.
The boundary is whether what is bought is a physical item or an act performed.

items.prompt: Explain how an intangible attribute allows a business to charge more than the physical product alone would earn.
items.canonical_answer: The buyer is not choosing between two physical products but between two bundles. Where one bundle carries a reputation for consistency and a shop that will replace a faulty item, the buyer's expected cost of a bad purchase is lower, so the buyer is prepared to pay more for the same physical thing - two near-identical bags of roasted beans can sell at N$85 and N$140. The advantage lasts because a rival can measure and match a physical feature within a production run, while a reputation is built out of years of consistent delivery. The mechanism runs only while the tangible performance keeps supporting the reputation; where the product stops delivering, the reputation decays and the premium goes with it.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must explain how the buyer's perceived risk or expected value changes, not simply assert that brands charge more.
The condition that performance must keep supporting the reputation is required.

items.prompt: Explain why product development matters to a business that is currently profitable.
items.canonical_answer: Because current profitability is a statement about products that are ageing. Tastes, technology and competitors move, so existing products tend to lose appeal, and a business with nothing prepared finds revenue falling with no replacement ready. Development is how the gap is filled before it opens. It can also open a segment the business does not reach, support a higher price where the improvement is one buyers value, use spare capacity, and reduce dependence on a single product - all of which matter most while the business still has the earnings to pay for them.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a small business of postponing product development for three years.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a business with one successful product and no successor in preparation. In the first year nothing visible happens and profit is higher, because the development spending was avoided. As rivals improve their offers and tastes move, the product's sales begin to slip, so revenue and contribution fall. The business now needs a replacement, but development takes time and money, and the money has to come from earnings that are already falling or from external finance that is harder to obtain once results are weakening. The consequence is that development starts later, costs more relative to what the business can afford, and arrives after the revenue gap has opened. The effect on the business is a squeeze on cash at the moment it is investing, which may force it to cut the promotion supporting the old product and deepen the fall. This chain is likely rather than certain: a product in a stable market with weak competition may hold its sales for far longer than three years.
marking_guidance: The starting condition - one ageing product, no successor - must be stated.
The mechanism must run through why the money and the time both become harder to find.
The consequence must be traced to cash and to the revenue gap, not asserted.
The chain must reach an effect on the business rather than stopping at lower sales.

items.prompt: Analyse how successful product differentiation affects the price a business can charge.
items.canonical_answer: Start from the condition that the difference is one buyers value and that rivals have not matched it. Where a product is undifferentiated, the nearest alternative is an equal substitute, so raising the price sends buyers to the rival and costs a great deal of volume. Differentiation removes that equality: switching now means giving something up, so a price rise costs less volume than it otherwise would. The mechanism is the buyer's reduced willingness to substitute, not the business's wish for a higher price. The consequence is that the business can hold a premium and earn more contribution for each unit sold, which supports the profit it needs to keep funding the difference. The chain reverses as soon as either condition fails: a difference nobody values changes no behaviour, and a difference that has been copied has stopped being a difference, which is why the premium has to be defended rather than banked.
marking_guidance: The condition - buyers value it and rivals have not copied it - must be stated, not assumed.
The mechanism must run through the buyer's willingness to substitute, because that is what changes.
The consequence must reach contribution for each unit rather than stopping at a higher price.
Must connect the result to the profit or competitive position of the business.

items.prompt: Analyse how a business's marketing mix changes as a product moves from growth into maturity.
items.canonical_answer: The condition that drives the change is that the market approaches saturation, so most people who will buy the product are already buying it and rivals have arrived. Promotion therefore shifts from persuading people to try the product to reminding existing buyers, because the job is no longer to win a new audience but to stay chosen by the one that exists. Price comes under pressure, because growth for one business now has to come out of another's share and price is one of the few remaining levers. Place is already wide, so the gain from further distribution is small. The product itself is varied - new sizes, flavours, a restyled pack - to hold interest in something the market has stopped finding new. items.prompt: A Namibian start-up is launching a bottled iced tea into a market where two imported brands sell at N$14 a bottle. It has N$900 000 of borrowed capital. Explain whether penetration pricing suits it.
items.canonical_answer: The market facts favour it: two established imports at a known price and a product that is not strongly differentiated mean buyers compare on price, so a launch at, say, N$11 would buy trial that a matching price would not. The finance fact works the other way. Penetration earns a thin margin until volume builds, and the N$900 000 is borrowed, so the start-up is paying interest on money that is funding a gap rather than a return. The judgement therefore turns on how long the gap lasts: if the start-up can reach the volume that lowers its cost for each bottle within the period its borrowing allows, penetration suits it; if not, it is buying share it cannot hold long enough to profit from. A partial answer - launching low in Windhoek only, where distribution is cheapest - limits the cash at risk while testing whether the price actually moves buyers.

items.prompt: Explain why raising the price after a penetration launch is difficult.
items.canonical_answer: Because the buyers the strategy attracted came for the price. Penetration works by making the product cheap enough to try, so a large part of the volume gained is made up of price-sensitive buyers who compare, which means the rise sends some of them back to the alternative. The launch price also becomes the reference point: buyers judge the new price against what they last paid rather than against the rival's price, so a rise reads as the product becoming expensive even where it remains good value. And a low launch price can fix the product as a cheap one in buyers' minds, which limits what it can charge later even after it improves.
marking_guidance: The difficulty must be developed through the type of buyer the low price attracted.
Reward the point about the launch price becoming the buyer's reference point.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a small manufacturer with limited finance should use penetration pricing to launch a new product.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: only where it can name the date by which volume must arrive and can finance the gap to that date. The decisive criterion is the business's cash, not the marketing logic. Penetration deliberately accepts a thin margin, so the strategy is a period of funded loss followed by a position worth having; a manufacturer with limited finance is buying that position with money it may need for stock and wages. The market conditions still have to hold as well - demand sensitive to price, a product not strongly differentiated, and the capacity to supply the volume created - and a small manufacturer commonly fails the last of those, turning a successful launch into unfilled orders. The strongest argument the other way is that a small business entering an established market has little else to offer: it cannot outspend the incumbents on promotion, and price is the one lever it fully controls. So the recommendation is conditional: launch low in one region rather than nationally, set the volume and the date at which the price rises, and stop if the volume has not come, because the alternative is a permanently cheap product financed by borrowing.

items.prompt: Analyse how price skimming allows a business to recover development spending quickly.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is a product that is genuinely new or distinctive, with something delaying imitation such as a patent or scarce know-how. Given that, there is a group of buyers who value having the product early and compare it with nothing else, because nothing else exists. A high launch price therefore loses little volume among those buyers while earning a large margin on each sale. The mechanism is that margin, not volume, is doing the work: a small number of sales at a wide margin returns cash sooner than a large number at a narrow one. As that group is served, each staged reduction opens the product to a further group, so revenue continues from buyers who would not have paid the launch price. The consequence is that the development spending is recovered from early cash flows rather than over years, which matters to the business because it reduces how long that money is tied up and how much borrowing the project needs. Where imitation is not delayed, rivals arrive at the wide margin and the chain stops at the first stage.
marking_guidance: The condition - distinctiveness and something delaying imitation - must open the chain.
The mechanism must be margin rather than volume, with the reason why the early group accepts the price.
The consequence must reach the timing of the cash recovered, not simply a higher price.
The chain must end on what this does for the business's finance, and what happens when the condition fails.

items.prompt: Explain how charging two different fares for the same journey can raise a bus operator's total revenue.
items.canonical_answer: Suppose 300 commuters would pay N$25 at peak and 120 midday passengers would pay no more than N$15. A single fare of N$25 earns 300 x N$25 = N$7 500 and carries nobody at midday. A single fare of N$15 carries all 420 but earns 420 x N$15 = N$6 300, because the commuters who would have paid N$25 now pay N$15. Charging N$25 at peak and N$15 off-peak earns N$7 500 + N$1 800 = N$9 300. The mechanism is that the operator keeps the high price from the buyers who would pay it while still making the sales it would otherwise lose, and it works here because the clock separates the groups, the groups differ in how much the journey matters to them, and a seat at 11 a.m. cannot be resold for 7 a.m.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must show why a single price gives up revenue at one end or the other.
The arithmetic must be shown, because the size of the gain is the point.
The three conditions must be identified in the example rather than asserted separately.

items.prompt: Analyse how dynamic pricing raises the revenue an airline earns from a fixed number of seats.
items.canonical_answer: The condition is capacity that is fixed and perishable: once the aircraft doors close, an empty seat earns nothing and cannot be sold later. Demand for a given flight also varies with how close departure is and with the season, and the airline can observe both through its booking system. When bookings are slow the price is lowered far enough to sell seats that would otherwise fly empty, and because the cost of carrying one more passenger is small, almost all of that fare is contribution. When bookings are strong the price rises, capturing what late and less flexible travellers are prepared to pay rather than selling those seats at the early fare. The mechanism is matching the price to the value of the remaining seat at each moment. The consequence is more revenue from the same aircraft than any single posted price would produce, and the effect on the business is a higher contribution towards the fixed cost of operating the flight. The chain depends on demand genuinely varying in an observable way, and on travellers not simply learning to wait for the price to fall.

items.prompt: Explain how a price of N$99.95 is intended to work differently from a price of N$100.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is how the figure is read rather than what it costs. A buyer scanning prices takes the leading digits first, so N$99.95 is filed as 'ninety-something' and N$100 as 'a hundred', and the two land in different mental price bands although the difference is five cents. The ending also carries a second signal, because prices ending in .95 or .99 are associated with value rather than with premium goods, so the figure tells the buyer what kind of product this is as well as what it costs. The business gives up five cents on each unit to move the price across a band boundary.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be the buyer's reading of the digits, not an assertion that the price looks cheaper.
Reward the second signal - what the ending says about the product's position.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of relying on psychological pricing.
items.canonical_answer: It suits some positions and works against others. A price ending in .95 signals a value product, so a private clinic pricing a consultation at N$899.95 or a jeweller pricing a ring at N$24 999.95 undermines the premium position the rest of the mix is building, because the ending is read as a discount cue. Experienced buyers may also see through the device, so the gain is small where buyers compare carefully. And the high-price form of psychological pricing - letting the price stand as a signal of quality - holds only while the product supports the claim, because a buyer disappointed at a high price is harder to recover than one disappointed at a low one.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed with a case where the device works against the business, because the ending carries a position as well as a number.

items.prompt: Explain why a business states the objective of a promotion campaign before choosing its methods.
items.canonical_answer: Because the method follows from the objective, and the same money spent on the wrong method achieves nothing measurable. A campaign whose purpose is trial of a new product needs sampling and introductory offers, which put the product in the buyer's hand; a campaign whose purpose is to defend share in maturity needs reminder advertising, which keeps a familiar product in view. Stating the objective also decides how the spending will be judged afterwards - a target of shifting a stated quantity in a stated period can be checked, while a general wish to raise the profile cannot - and it is the reason methods are combined rather than chosen singly, since advertising and sales promotion do different jobs.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a small business with a limited budget should spend it on sales promotion rather than on advertising.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: sales promotion first, with a share held back for something that lasts. The decisive criterion is that a limited budget has to produce a result the business can see and afford to have measured. Sales promotion acts within weeks, its cost is known in advance, and the response can be counted, which suits a business that cannot carry an uncertain outcome. Advertising is paid for before the result is known, builds slowly, and is hard to separate from other causes, so a small budget spread across a medium may buy too little repetition to register at all. The strongest argument the other way is that sales promotion buys a burst and builds nothing: the effect largely stops when the offer stops, the discount is given on units that would have sold anyway, and repeated offers train buyers to wait, which lowers the price the product can hold. So the recommendation is conditional: use promotion to get trial, keep part of the budget for something that accumulates - packaging, a consistent brand presence online - and judge the campaign on sales in the month after the offer rather than during it.
marking_guidance: A judgement between the two is required.

The advantage holds where the audience the medium delivers matches the target market - a national campaign for a product sold in one town pays for reach it cannot use, so its cost for each person who could actually buy is high.

items.prompt: Explain why the sales figure recorded during a promotional offer overstates what the offer has won.
items.canonical_answer: The incentive lowers the cost, or raises the value, of buying now rather than later. That moves two kinds of purchase into the offer period: buyers who were going to buy next month buy this month instead, and buyers who would have bought a rival's product switch for as long as the offer runs. Only the second group is new business, and even that lasts only if the trial converts to repeat purchase. The first group is buying that would have happened anyway, so the sales recorded during the offer include volume taken from the following period, which is why the honest test is what sales do across the offer and the month after it together, compared with the same stretch without an offer.

items.prompt: Explain why running a discount offer every month can weaken a business.
items.canonical_answer: It changes what buyers believe the product is worth. Regular offers teach buyers to wait for the next one, so purchases concentrate in the discount weeks and the full price becomes a number few people pay - the product's real price has quietly fallen to the offer price. Meanwhile the discount is given on every unit sold during the offer, including those that would have sold at full price, so the cost is much larger than the discount on the additional sales alone. The business ends with lower revenue for each unit, a buying pattern it has to keep feeding, and a price it can no longer raise without losing the volume it created.

items.prompt: Explain why packaging is treated as part of promotion and not only as part of the product.
items.canonical_answer: Because of where it does its work. On a supermarket shelf the pack is the last message a buyer sees before choosing, so its colour, shape and name act as a silent advertisement at the moment of decision, and they connect the product to whatever the buyer already knows of the brand. That is why a business that changes a pack design without warning loses sales from regular buyers who cannot find the product they were looking for. Packaging also positions the product: a resealable pack, a single-household portion size or a heavier material that feels expensive each change what the product is worth to a buyer without changing what is inside it.

items.prompt: Explain one argument against investing in more elaborate packaging.
items.canonical_answer: It adds cost to every unit and waste to every sale. Unlike a campaign, which is paid for once, packaging is a cost carried by each item the business ever sells, so a few dollars added to a pack is subtracted from the contribution of every unit for as long as the design lasts. The waste side has become commercial as well as environmental: buyers and regulators in many countries now weigh how much material a product arrives in, so elaborate packaging can work against the position it was meant to build. The business therefore balances the promotional gain against the cost for each unit and against the reaction to the waste.
marking_guidance: The argument must be developed through the fact that the cost recurs on every unit, because that is what separates it from a one-off campaign.
Reward the point that waste has become a commercial consideration.

items.prompt: Explain how a recognised brand makes a business's other promotion work harder.
items.canonical_answer: The mechanism is what the audience already holds. An advertisement for an unknown product has to establish who is speaking, what the product is and why it should be believed before it can say anything else, so most of the message is spent on groundwork. An advertisement for a recognised brand starts from a name the audience can already place, so the same space can be spent on the offer itself and the message registers faster. The brand also lowers the risk the buyer feels, because it carries a promise that this purchase will be like the last one, which matters most for services, where nothing can be inspected in advance. The result is more effect for the same spending - which is also why the effect runs backwards when the promise is broken.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be the recognition the audience already holds and what it saves the message from doing.
Reward the perceived-risk point and the observation that the mechanism can reverse.

items.prompt: Explain why a strong brand can make a quality failure more damaging rather than less.
items.canonical_answer: Because what the failure breaks is the promise the brand carries. A buyer of an unknown product who receives a poor item has learned little, since nothing was promised. A buyer of a well-known brand has chosen it precisely to avoid that outcome, so the failure contradicts the reason for the purchase, and the more buyers who held that expectation, the more of them are disappointed at once. The asymmetry is the point: the promise is built out of years of consistent delivery and a single widely reported failure can undo a large part of it. Where the product stops delivering what the brand claims, the brand speeds up the loss of custom rather than slowing it.
marking_guidance: The limitation must be developed through the expectation the brand created, because that is what makes the failure worse.

items.prompt: A Namibian manufacturer makes cooldrink, a professional-grade paint and electric bicycles. Explain the difference between intensive, selective and exclusive distribution for these three products.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is how many outlets carry the product, which trades availability against the producer's control over how it is sold. Cooldrink suits intensive distribution: it is bought on impulse, so it needs to be in as many outlets as possible. The professional paint suits selective distribution through a limited number of trade merchants whose staff can advise contractors. The electric bicycles suit exclusive distribution through one dealer per town, which protects the dealer's margin and the standard of servicing at the cost of being harder to find.

items.prompt: Analyse the effect on a producer of adding a wholesaler to its distribution channel.
items.canonical_answer: The starting condition is a producer selling directly to a small number of retailers it can reach itself. Adding a wholesaler gives the product access to outlets the producer could not serve - the wholesaler already calls on them, holds stock, breaks bulk and often extends them credit - so the number of shops carrying the product rises and volume rises with it. The mechanism on the other side is that the wholesaler is paid out of the price: it takes a margin, so the producer's revenue for each unit falls, and the producer also loses some control over the shelf price and the way the product is presented. The consequence is two movements in opposite directions, and whether the producer ends better off depends on which moves further - a producer whose volume doubles through a wholesaler taking 12% is ahead, while one whose volume rises slightly through a wholesaler taking 30% is not. The effect on the business also includes losing direct contact with the trade, so it learns about a problem only when the wholesaler's order falls.

The mechanism must run both ways, because reach rises and revenue for each unit falls.
The consequence must be stated as depending on which movement is larger, with figures to show it.
The chain must end on the effect on the business, including the loss of contact.

items.prompt: A Windhoek food producer supplies shops in Oshakati, Katima Mulilo and Luderitz. Evaluate whether it should use a wholesaler or distribute directly.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: use a wholesaler for the distant towns and keep direct supply for Windhoek. The decisive criterion is the full cost of serving a scattered retail base directly, not the wholesaler's margin alone. Reaching Katima Mulilo, Oshakati and Luderitz from Windhoek means vehicles, drivers, fuel over very long distances, and a sales presence in each region; that whole cost is what the margin has to be compared with, and for a producer of this size the wholesaler will usually be cheaper for the distant towns. The strongest argument against is contact: a producer that never meets its retailers learns nothing about why the product is or is not selling and hears about a problem only when an order falls, and it also gives up control of the shelf price. That argument is strongest close to home, where the cost of calling on shops is low, which is why the split answer is better than either pure option. The recommendation depends on the margin quoted and on the producer keeping some direct contact with the trade; if the wholesaler's margin approaches what own distribution would cost, or if the product needs explaining at the shelf, direct supply becomes the better choice.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a small retailer in a country with long distances between towns should build an e-commerce operation.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: build it, but as a way of taking orders rather than as a promise of national delivery. The decisive criterion is the cost of the final stage of the physical journey, because that is what the retailer cannot avoid and cannot reduce much. Where towns are hundreds of kilometres apart, the courier charge on a single low-value order can approach the value of the order, so an unrestricted delivery offer loses money on exactly the orders it attracts. The counterargument is strong and should be conceded: an online presence reaches customers who were unlikely to visit the shop, it costs little to set up compared with opening a branch, and a retailer that stays offline in a market where buyers search online is invisible to them. The resolution is in the design rather than in the decision - collection points, a minimum order value for free delivery, consolidated weekly runs to each town, and digital delivery for any part of the range that can travel as data. The recommendation depends on the retailer being able to price delivery honestly; if it has to absorb the freight to look competitive, the operation will lose money as it grows.

items.prompt: Okahandja Tiles makes one paving slab. Its variable cost is N$18 a slab, its fixed costs are N$96 000 a month and it currently makes 12 000 slabs a month, which is its normal output. It prices at full cost plus a 40% mark-up. A competitor has begun selling a similar slab at N$32. Calculate the full cost, the cost-plus price, and the monthly profit at 12 000 slabs under each of the two prices if volume holds; calculate the output needed to break even at the cost-plus price; and evaluate whether Okahandja Tiles should match the competitor.
items.canonical_answer:
Full cost. Fixed cost a slab at normal output = N$96 000 / 12 000 = N$8. Full cost = N$18 + N$8 = N$26.

Cost-plus price. Mark-up = N$26 x 0.40 = N$10.40, so the price = N$26 + N$10.40 = N$36.40.

Profit at N$36.40, if 12 000 slabs still sell. Contribution = N$36.40 - N$18 = N$18.40 a slab. Total contribution = N$18.40 x 12 000 = N$220 800. Profit = N$220 800 - N$96 000 = N$124 800.

Profit at N$32, with volume held at 12 000. Contribution = N$32 - N$18 = N$14 a slab. Total contribution = N$14 x 12 000 = N$168 000. Profit = N$168 000 - N$96 000 = N$72 000.

Break-even at the cost-plus price = N$96 000 / N$18.40 = 5 218 slabs, against 12 000 now.

Judgement: do not match at N$32. The decisive criterion is how much volume the N$4.40 difference actually costs, and the break-even figure shows how much room there is: at N$36.40 the business covers its fixed costs at 5 218 slabs, so it can lose 6 782 slabs of monthly volume - more than half - before it stops covering its fixed costs at all. Matching, by contrast, gives up N$52 800 of profit a month immediately and with certainty, because it is given away on all 12 000 slabs including those that would have sold anyway. The point at which matching becomes the better option is where holding the price leaves profit below N$72 000, which needs contribution of N$168 000 at N$18.40 a slab, or 9 131 slabs - a fall of 2 869 slabs, about 24% of current volume. The strongest argument for matching is that slabs are close to a commodity and builders compare prices directly, so a gap of N$4.40 - 14% above the competitor's price - may well move more than 24% of the volume; that is exactly what the business does not know and should find out before acting. The recommendation therefore depends on evidence about buyer response - what happened at the last price change, and whether the competitor's slab is genuinely comparable in thickness and finish. If the slabs are identical and builders switch freely, a partial reduction towards N$34 keeps more of the margin than a full match while closing most of the visible gap.
marking_guidance: Every figure must be calculated with the working shown.
Judgement: the answer must recommend, not set out both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on this business's own break-even and margin figures rather than on cost-plus in the abstract.
Criterion: the decisive factor is how much volume the price difference would have to cost before matching is worthwhile, and that volume must be calculated rather than estimated.
Counterargument: must address the fact that slabs are near-commodity and the price gap is visible.
Condition: must name the evidence that would settle the decision.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Namib Snacks sells three products. Its oldest line provides 62% of revenue and its volume has been flat for four years. Its newest line, launched 18 months ago, is growing at 40% a year but holds 7% of a market whose leader holds 33%. The business has N$700 000 to allocate. Evaluate how it should divide that money between an extension strategy for the oldest line and support for the newest.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: put the larger share behind the newest line, with a defined minimum held back to defend the oldest, and make the split conditional on why the oldest line's volume is flat.

Paragraph 1 - read the two positions. Flat volume over four years places the oldest line in maturity; at 62% of revenue it is the business's earner and its main exposure. The newest line is growing at 40% but holds 7% against a leader on 33%, so it is a question mark: the market is attractive and the product is not winning it yet.

Paragraph 2 - what each use of the money buys. An extension strategy on the oldest line - new variants, repackaging, a fresh campaign - is cheap because it uses machinery and distribution already in place, and it defends 62% of revenue. Support for the newest line is buying share from a much larger rival, which is expensive and slow, but it is the only candidate to replace the earner when maturity turns into decline.

Paragraph 3 - the decisive criterion. Why is the oldest line flat? If it is tired promotion or a dated pack, extension can recover growth cheaply and deserves real money. If buyers have moved to a different kind of snack, extension postpones a decision the business has already left four years late, and the money belongs behind the successor.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest counterargument. Starving the oldest line risks the 62% that pays for everything, and a business that loses its earner while backing a question mark can end with neither. That is why the answer is a split rather than a choice, and why the defensive share should be set first.

Judgement and conditions: allocate the larger share to the newest line, keep enough on the oldest to hold distribution and shelf presence, and make the extension spending conditional on research showing a recoverable cause. Review after a year against share in the growing market, not against total sales, because total sales will be dominated by the older line either way.

Context: the plan must use Namib Snacks' own facts - 62% of revenue, four flat years, 7% against a leader on 33%, and the N$700 000.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be why the oldest line's volume is flat.
Counterargument: must include the risk of starving the line that pays for the business.
Condition: must end on what would change the split and how it would be reviewed.

items.prompt: Erongo Tours runs day trips from Swakopmund. Two thirds of its customers are international visitors who book before arriving; the rest are Namibian families booking within a week of travelling. It has N$120 000 for promotion over a year and its vehicles run at about half capacity from May to August. Analyse the circumstances under which each promotion method would suit Erongo Tours, and evaluate how it should spend the money.
items.canonical_answer:
The two customer groups are reached in different places, and that is what the analysis turns on.

International visitors book before they arrive, so nothing in Swakopmund reaches them. They are found through search results, the operator's own website, review platforms and the listings of the lodges and agents they book through. Digital promotion suits them precisely because it can be targeted by location and interest, is counted, and can be bought in small amounts - all of which a N$120 000 annual budget needs. Advertising in the ordinary sense is the wrong tool here: the audience is scattered across several countries, so any medium that would reach it delivers mostly people who are unlikely to travel to Namibia, and the cost for each usable contact would be very high.

Namibian families book within a week, which makes them a different problem: they can be reached locally and they respond to a deadline. Radio and social media both work for them, and a sales promotion - a reduced family rate for May to August - attacks the specific fact that vehicles run at half capacity in those months. Because a seat on a departed vehicle earns nothing, almost any fare above the cost of carrying one more passenger is worth taking in those months, which is what makes a seasonal offer sound here rather than merely cheap.

The limits have to be set against that. A sales promotion repeated every winter teaches families to wait for it, so the offer should be tied to the season and the capacity rather than made a permanent second price list. Digital reach depends on platforms Erongo does not control, so the spending should build its own website and review presence as well as buying advertisements.

Recommendation: spend roughly two thirds on digital promotion aimed at the international group, because that is where two thirds of the customers are and where the money can be traced, and the remainder on a winter campaign for the domestic group carrying a seasonal family rate. The decisive criterion is where each group actually makes its decision, which for one is before arrival and for the other is a week beforehand. The strongest argument against the split is that it spreads a small budget across two campaigns and may be too thin for either, which is why the domestic spending should be concentrated into the May to August window rather than run all year. The recommendation depends on Erongo measuring bookings by source; if the digital spending cannot be traced to bookings within the first season, the balance should move towards the domestic campaign, where the response is easier to see.

items.prompt: A producer is deciding whether to distribute its own product or to sell through a wholesaler. Identify the questions it should answer before deciding, and explain what each one tells it.
items.canonical_answer:
What would it cost to do this ourselves? State the whole cost, not the fuel: vehicles, drivers, fuel over the actual distances, a sales presence in each region, and the stock held to serve it. That total is what the wholesaler's margin has to be compared with, and producers routinely compare the margin against nothing.

What margin does the wholesaler take, and what does it do for it? Holding stock, breaking bulk, calling on outlets we could not reach and extending credit to retailers are real services. A margin paid for delivery alone is worth less than the same margin paid for access to 300 shops.

How many outlets do we need the product to be in? Each business the product passes through takes a share of the price, so the producer's revenue for each unit falls as the channel lengthens. Where the product is bought on impulse and has to be everywhere, that is a price worth paying; where a few outlets are enough, it is not.

How much control do we need over price and presentation? A longer channel means the shelf price and the way the product is displayed are decided by someone else. For a premium product, losing that control can cost more than the margin.

How will we hear about problems? A producer that never meets its retailers learns about a difficulty only when the wholesaler's order falls. Keeping some direct contact is a condition of using an intermediary well, not an alternative to it.

Does any part of this travel as data? If part of what the business sells can be delivered over a network, that part needs no channel at all, and the question only applies to the physical range.
marking_guidance: State each question plainly before explaining it.
Give the reason each question matters - what a wrong answer would cost the producer.
Use the context: these are the questions a producer asks about its own channel, not a general account of intermediaries, and each answer should say what it tells the business.

items.prompt: A 24-room lodge is open 20 nights in February, giving 480 room-nights. At a single published rate of N$1 600 it expects to sell 160 room-nights. It believes that adding a resident rate of N$950 would sell a further 180 room-nights without losing any of the 160. Servicing an occupied room costs N$240 a night. Calculate the revenue under each arrangement and the extra contribution the resident rate would earn, and evaluate whether the lodge should introduce it.
items.canonical_answer:
Single rate. Revenue = N$1 600 x 160 = N$256 000.

Two rates. Resident revenue = N$950 x 180 = N$171 000, so total revenue = N$256 000 + N$171 000 = N$427 000.

Extra contribution from the resident rate. Contribution on each resident night = N$950 - N$240 = N$710. Total = N$710 x 180 = N$127 800 a month of February trading, earned from rooms that would otherwise have stood empty.

Judgement: introduce the resident rate. The decisive criterion is that the capacity is perishable - 320 of the 480 room-nights would earn nothing at all under the single rate - so any rate above the N$240 cost of servicing the room adds contribution towards costs the lodge pays whether the room is occupied or not. The three conditions for discriminating also hold: residents can be separated by an identity document at check-in, the two groups differ in price sensitivity because an international visitor has already paid for the flight while a resident has cheaper alternatives at home, and the booking cannot be resold because the name is checked on arrival. The strongest argument against is the assumption the calculation rests on: it assumes none of the 160 international room-nights moves to the lower rate. If the rate is published without a check, or if agents book residents' rooms, that assumption fails - and every international night that switches costs N$650 of revenue, so 40 switched nights would remove N$26 000 and cut the gain by a fifth. The recommendation therefore depends on the check at arrival being real, and on the resident rate being confined to the low season; extending it into July, when the rooms would sell at N$1 600 anyway, turns the same scheme from filling empty rooms into discounting full ones.
marking_guidance: Every figure must be calculated with the working shown, and each must carry its unit or currency.
Judgement: a recommendation is required, not a presentation of both arrangements.
Context: the recommendation must rest on this lodge's own February occupancy and servicing cost.
Criterion: the decisive factor is that unsold room-nights are perishable and earn nothing.
Counterargument: must address the assumption that no international booking switches to the lower rate, with the cost of switching calculated.
Condition: must state what would make the scheme stop working.

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: Etosha Leather sells handmade bags at N$2 400 through one shop in Windhoek and at craft markets. A national retail chain has offered to stock the bags in 14 stores if the price to the chain is N$1 100 a bag. Evaluate whether Etosha Leather should accept.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: decline for the main handmade line, and offer the chain a separate, simpler line at a price that covers its own costs - unless Etosha can produce at a volume and cost the N$1 100 supports without changing the bag.

Paragraph 1 - what the current mix is doing. The N$2 400 price, the single shop and the craft-market setting all say the same thing about the product, and the buyer reads them together. The premium rests on that consistency as much as on the leather.

Paragraph 2 - what the offer changes. Fourteen chain stores change place, and place changes the rest. On a chain shelf nobody explains the bag, so the packaging and the brand mark have to carry the whole message, and the pack becomes the last thing the buyer sees before choosing. The chain's shelf price will also be visible beside mass-produced bags, which invites a comparison the craft market never made.

Paragraph 3 - the decisive criterion. Can Etosha supply 14 stores at N$1 100 while the bag remains the bag that justifies N$2 400? If it can only do so by using thinner leather or faster methods, the offer destroys the differentiation it is trying to exploit, and the brand carries the disappointment back to the Windhoek shop.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest argument for accepting. Fourteen stores are reach no craft market can give, the brand becomes recognised nationally, and volume lowers cost for each bag, which is exactly how a small producer grows. A refusal keeps a premium on a very small base.

Judgement and conditions: accept it in the form of a separate line with its own name and materials, so the handmade line's position is not contradicted; or decline and use the shop and the markets to build national recognition more slowly. Reconsider if Etosha can raise output without changing the product, or if the chain will take the bags at a price nearer the current one.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay - structure with a stated judgement is what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must use Etosha's own facts - the N$2 400 price, one shop and craft markets, and the N$1 100 offer across 14 stores.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be whether the product can be supplied at that price without losing what justifies the premium.
Counterargument: must include the genuine case for accepting - reach, recognition and volume.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer.
